newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russians hope to fix Mir before Shuttle arrives.
newsitem.headline: Russians hope to fix Mir before Shuttle arrives.

text.p: Two cosmonauts due to reach the crippled Mir space station in two weeks time hope to finish risky repairs before a U.S. space shuttle docks with it in mid-September, Russian space officials said on Thursday.
Mission director Vladimir Solovyov said work to restore the power supply, damaged in a collision a month ago, would start soon after the cosmonauts arrive on Mir in August 7.

"In the first few days after the new crew gets to Mir, we plan to start restoring the power supply. I think it will work out before the shuttle arrives," he told reporters at Korolyov Mission Control outside Moscow.
"Scientific experiments, the main purpose of our missions and foreign missions to Mir, are pointless until the power supply is restored."

Solovyov was clearly responding to remarks on Wednesday by U.S. President Bill Clinton's top science adviser, Jack Gibbons, who said Mir's power problems could prevent U.S. astronaut Wendy Lawrence taking a turn on Mir from September 20.

Russian Space Agency chief Yuri Koptev told a news conference the collision on June 25 that knocked out half Mir's power supply may mean a loss of three to four months from the experimental programme on the station and cost $15-20 million to repair -- money his civilian body simply did not have.

Accepting that a failure to restore power could mean the end of lucrative cooperation with the Americans, Koptev said he would be looking to the Russian government to help out, either from its special reserve fund for disasters or by reducing the extent of planned cuts in the space agency's 1997 budget.

When a cargo craft punctured the Spektr scientific module, the crew had to hurriedly disconnect cables from its solar panels, a major source of power on the station. British-born NASA physicist Michael Foale had to suspend many experiments.
NASA could decide whether or not to send Foale's replacement to Mir as late as a day before the shuttle leaves, Gibbons said.
Lawrence, a 37-year-old U.S. Navy commander, is in training at Star City outside Moscow for a four-month stint on Mir.

The Russian relief crew, mission commander Anatoly Solovyov and flight engineer Pavel Vinogradov, will put on spacesuits to enter Spektr to carry out the repairs. They trained on Thursday in a pool at Star City, simulating the repairs.
Koptev said they may make up to five more spacewalks as a team outside the station to inspect the hole punched in Spektr and then to try to repair it.

The tiny puncture could simply be in the skin of the module, which would be relatively straightforward to repair. But it may be a more complex rupture involving the mounting of one of Spektr's solar panels, which was wrecked in the collision.
The U.S. shuttle Atlantis may bring up extra equipment for repairs and Russian cosmonaut Vladimir Titov, who will fly on it, may also take part in a spacewalk to help out, Koptev said.

The Mir relief crew spent two days at the Baikonur cosmodrome inspecting the Soyuz TM-26 spacecraft that will blast off from there on August 5 and take them into space. The three-man crew on Mir are preparing for their arrival.

"They have to clean up the station a bit, make preparations for better orientation in space for the new Soyuz to dock, and make all life support systems work under the bigger load they will have when five men are aboard," Vladimir Solovyov said.

Mir commander Vasily Tsibliyev, who developed an irregular heartbeat, is still taking medicine despite an improvement in his condition. But he is in shape to fly himself and Russian flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin back to Earth on August 14.
